opening.headline: Among several candidates, we decide which embedding model and dimension to use, considering accuracy, storage cost, delay, and replacement cost.
body: Once an embedding model is set, it cannot be easily changed. That's because all the document vectors you've already created are tied to that model. So your initial choice greatly influences subsequent costs.

In this lesson, we'll look at how to compare the three candidates in terms of accuracy, cost, and latency, and explain why a full reindex is necessary when replacing a model. Finally, we organize the selection sequence that follows from organizing requirements to recording.
opening.objectivesLead: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to:
objectives: Accuracy, storage cost, and delay requirements can be categorized as selection criteria.
Can determine the suitability of a candidate model

screens.title: There are many candidates, but you have to choose one.
screens.lead: Compare and read the three candidate cards. Find out what needs are pulling in different directions.

visual.alt: A scene showing three candidate model cards and three requirement chips above them.

paragraphs: A team must decide on an embedding model to use for in-house document retrieval. Candidate A has high accuracy, but the vector is large and requires a lot of storage space. Candidate B is balanced. Candidate C has lower delay and cost, but slightly lower accuracy.

Requirements also pull in different directions. Search quality must be high, storage costs must be within budget, and responses must be fast. There is usually no candidate who satisfies the best of all three.

There is an added burden here. Once an embedding model is set, the cost of changing it is high. This is because if you change the model, you will have to recreate all the document vectors you have already created. This class covers how to evaluate candidates by setting criteria and making choices by considering replacement costs.

callout.label: Things to think about
callout.text: Is choosing the candidate with the highest accuracy always the right answer? If you need to change the model after selection, check in class what will change.

screens.outro: First, let's recall what we did with the existing vectors when changing the model.

screens.title: Recall how we processed existing vectors
screens.lead: When you select each question, the instructor's thoughts unfold. You won't have to enter or submit your answer, so think of it first and then press it.

items.prompt: How do I handle existing vectors when changing models?
items.answer: The safest way is to re-embed all documents with the new model and create a new index. Leaving the existing vector as is and changing only some of it will result in inconsistent comparisons, harming search quality. This lesson explains why.

items.prompt: Have you ever mixed up vectors from a new model with old vectors?
items.answer: If you mix them up, distance calculations lose their meaning. This is because the space where the vector is placed is different for each model. The danger is that the search works on the surface, making it difficult to notice the problem.

items.prompt: Have you ever estimated the cost of reindexing?
items.answer: The reindex cost is a call cost proportional to the number of documents and number of tokens. OpenAI charges based on the number of input tokens. If you estimate ahead of time, you can treat replacement as a planned task.

screens.outro: Now that we've summarized our experience, let's look at how candidates compare by criteria.

screens.title: Compare candidates by accuracy, cost, and delay
screens.lead: The table below summarizes the characteristics of the candidate models in the document in the same column. In each row, read which criteria are strong and which criteria are weak.

data.notes: The numbers in the table are from the conditions set by the supplier. There is no guarantee that our data and queries will result in the same ranking, so it should only be used to narrow down candidates and final comparisons should be measured directly with the same set of queries. Dimensions are also cost items. Reducing it can make storage and retrieval easier, but can reduce accuracy, so measure candidates and dimensions together. For example, if you compare 1024 dimensions and 256 dimensions in the same model, you can directly see how much the accuracy changes, as the storage amount differs by about 4 times. Putting accuracy, storage, and delay side by side in one table makes the rationale for your choice clear.

screens.outro: Now that we have completed the comparison by criteria, let us explain why model replacement requires a full reindex.

screens.title: Commentary: Why a full reindex is necessary when replacing a model
screens.lead: The instructor explains step by step the process by which the vector spaces of the old model and the new model are misaligned. Select the right arrow to proceed to the next step. Learners do not enter answers.

visual.alt: The vector space of the old model and the vector space of the new model are in different coordinate systems, and the document vector and query vector do not match each other.
labels: Vector space of the old model
Vector space of the new model
Distance is meaningless because they are different spaces.

steps.title: Situation: Only the query was changed to the new model.
steps.body: One team replaced the embedding model with a new model. To save costs, we left the document vector as is and only embedded the query into a new model. Since the dimensions are the same, the code runs without error.

steps.title: Vector space is different for each model
steps.body: Embeddings translate meaning into coordinates based on how the model learned it. Different models place the same sentence in different coordinate systems. Even if the dimensions are the same, what each number means is different for each model.

steps.title: Old document vectors and new query vectors cannot be compared
steps.body: Distance is only meaningful when two vectors are in the same space. The distance between the new model's query vector and the old model's document vector is just a random number. Searches return results, but rankings lose meaning.

steps.title: So we re-embed all the documents
steps.body: To use a new model, you must re-embed all documents into the new model and create a new index. If you change just a few parts, different spaces will be mixed within one index. When changing settings such as task type, you need to recreate the document vector for the same reason.

steps.title: Estimate the cost of reindexing
steps.body: OpenAI charges requests based on the number of input tokens. Assuming the document is 1 million pages and approximately 800 tokens per page, the throughput per dollar of document is approximately $16 for small and approximately $104 for large. This value is only the call cost and is separate from the index rebuild time and conversion operations.

steps.title: Treat replacement as a planned task
steps.body: Therefore, the initial choice is important, and replacement must be done as a planned operation with a set schedule and cost. By creating a new index next to the old index and switching after confirming it with evaluation, you can avoid broken searches in the middle.

screens.outro: Now that you understand replacement costs, let's outline your selection order.

screens.title: Explanation: Five steps from request organizing to recording
screens.lead: If you select and expand each item, you can see the basis for each step of the selection order. Please unfold them in order starting from number 1.

items.title: Step 1: Sorting out requirements: Decide on the most demanding items
items.body: First decide which is the tightest: your accuracy goal, acceptable delay, or storage budget. Since you can't get the best of all three at the same time, the most non-negotiable item becomes the first criterion to separate candidates.

items.title: Step 2: Narrow down the candidates: Reduce the candidates to around 3 using the documentation.
items.body: The Voyage 4 series is divided into large for highest quality, basic for balanced, and lite for delay and cost optimization, and you can choose from dimensions 256, 512, 1024, and 2048. In this way, we narrow down the candidates by the features of the manual, but also estimate the storage amount. Storage amount is number of documents x dimension x number size. For example, if you store 1 million numbers with 4 bytes per number, 1024 dimensions will be about 4 GB, and 256 dimensions will be about 1 GB, a four-fold difference.

items.title: Step 3 Measurement: Measure directly under the same conditions
items.body: By applying the same conditions to the candidates to the representative query and document set, we measure the rate at which the required documents are included in the top k. We also see the width that drops when the dimension is reduced. The supplier table is used to filter candidates, and the final basis is the measurement of our data.

items.title: Step 4 Replacement Cost: Estimate the cost of replacement in advance
items.body: Since changing the model is a full reindex, estimate the call cost in advance, which is proportional to the number of documents and tokens. The more expensive the model, the greater the burden of replacement. Also think about how many years you will use the model you choose.

items.title: Step 5: Record the basis for selection on one page
items.body: Accuracy, storage volume, delay, replacement cost and reasons for selection are listed on one page. With records, you can immediately see which assumptions were broken and reevaluate when your needs change.

screens.outro: I will summarize today's highlights in the last screen.

screens.title: Once you decide on an embedding, it is expensive to change.
screens.lead: The first question, whether it is okay to choose the candidate with the highest accuracy, is answered using the criteria learned today.

paragraphs: The criteria for selecting candidates are accuracy, storage cost, and delay. The three criteria pull in different directions, so we determine the most stringent needs first, narrow down the candidates that meet those needs, and then select them by measuring them with our data. The model with the highest accuracy is not always the right answer.

Once an embedding model is set, it is expensive to change. Because each model has a different vector space, if you change models, you cannot compare old document vectors with new query vectors and all documents must be re-embedded. The same applies when changing dimensions or task types.

Therefore, when making a choice, consider the replacement cost, and when replacement becomes necessary, treat it as a planned task of creating a new index, evaluating it, and then converting. The habit of keeping records of accuracy, storage volume, delays, replacement costs and reasons will speed up your next decision.

If we summarize it as a practical checklist, it is as follows. Have you written down what your most stringent demands are, measured your candidates with the same query, estimated the cost of reindexing, and recorded your rationale? If you can answer all four, you are ready to explain your choice.

callout.label: Based on one sentence
callout.text: The embedding is chosen by measurement and the cost of changing it is also calculated.

checks.intro: Think back to the comparison table you just saw and check for yourself. Results are not recorded.
checks.q: Candidate A has high accuracy and large vectors, and candidate C has low delay and cost. What is the best way to choose?
options: Select the model with the highest accuracy from the supplier table
Always choose the model with the lowest storage and delay.
Measure accuracy, storage amount, and delay together by measuring under the same conditions with representative queries and documents.
Choose the model with the most recent name
checks.correctFeedback: That's right. We can make a balanced choice by looking at the three criteria together as measurements of our data.
checks.incorrectFeedback: The choice to look at only one criterion misses other needs. Think again under what conditions the numbers in the table came from.
checks.explain: Since the numbers in the table are based on the supplier, we measure them again with our own data, and write down the accuracy, storage, delay, and replacement costs as a basis for selection.

wrong.0: Looking only at accuracy misses storage costs and latency requirements.
wrong.1: Looking only at cost misses the need for accuracy.
wrong.3: Being up-to-date does not guarantee performance on our data.

checks.intro: Please check the last question, remembering the reason for re-indexing seen in the commentary. Results are not recorded.
checks.q: I changed the model, but I left the old document vector as is and only embedded the query with the new model. What happens?
options: Since the vector space is different, distances lose meaning, so the entire document must be re-embedded.
If the dimensions are the same, there is no problem.
Searching is normal, storage capacity only increases.
This can be solved by embedding the query twice.
checks.correctFeedback: That's correct. Vectors in different spaces cannot be compared, requiring a full reindex.
checks.incorrectFeedback: That's not true. If the model is different, think again about the space where the vector is placed.
checks.explain: The vector space is different for each model. Comparing old document vectors with new query vectors is meaningless, so you need to re-embed all documents into the new model.

wrong.1: Even if the dimensions are the same, if the space is different, distance has no meaning.
wrong.2: It's a question of search quality, not storage capacity.
wrong.3: Spatial inconsistencies cannot be resolved by modifying only the query side.

glossary.def: Axes on which candidates are compared, such as accuracy, storage cost, and delay.
After changing the model, all documents are re-embedded into the new model and a new index is created.
This involves changing to a different embedding model. Reindexing is necessary for the same reason when changing dimensions or task types.
This is a method of evaluating and selecting directly based on our data and inquiries, not based on supplier figures.

misconceptions.myth: You can also compare the new model's query vector with the old document vector.
misconceptions.fact: Different models have different vector spaces, so distances lose meaning. If you change your model, you will need to re-embed all documents.

misconceptions.myth: The model with the highest evaluation performance is the correct answer.
misconceptions.fact: The supplier table is the value of the supplier condition. We need to look at it again in terms of our data, costs, and delays.

misconceptions.myth: Dimensions can be easily changed later.
misconceptions.fact: All stored vectors are made in that dimension, so changing them will affect them. Dimensions must also be chosen carefully along with model selection.

closing.lead: Summarizes what was covered in this class.
points: Once you decide on an embedding, it is expensive to change.
We look at accuracy, storage cost, and delay together and choose based on our data.
Replacing a model means a full reindex.
Keep records of the basis for selection and replacement costs.
